title: The first precept in Pali
hookLine: a ring of boys with sticks, a snake in the middle, and a man who stops
tomorrow: why doesn't the second precept just say don't steal?

lines: A RING OF BOYS, A SNAKE.
cards: A street in Savatthi. A ring of boys with sticks, and in the middle of the ring, a snake, twisting in the dust. A man walking his alms round stops.
Why are you beating it? We're scared it'll bite us, they say. The Dhammapada commentary tells it this way, and the man is the Buddha.
He doesn't threaten them. He doesn't hand down a law. He asks them to notice something about the snake: it wants to be happy, just like them.
That's the shape of the first precept. It's not a rule handed down from above. It's a rule you give yourself, so yes, still a rule, but yours.

teach.b: Here's the line people chant: panatipata veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami. Take it apart. Pana: living, breathing beings, not only people.
Sikkhapadam: a training step, from sikkha, training, and pada, a step or a foothold.

teach.h: NO ORDER: I TAKE IT UP.
teach.b: Samadiyami: I undertake, I take it up. Put together: I undertake the training to refrain from taking life. Notice what isn't there.
No thou shalt not. No one is giving an order; the speaker takes a step. A step can wobble, and you can take it again tomorrow.
And the reason under it is likeness.

teach.h: REMEMBER THAT YOU ARE LIKE THEM.
teach.b: In Max Müller's English, the Dhammapada says, "All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter."

The Buddha's verses for the boys go the same way: if you want happiness, don't take it from others who want it too. The snake and the boys share one thing, and so do you and whoever is in front of you.

how: In Theravada temples lay people often ask for the five precepts after the homage and the refuges; a monk chants each line and they repeat it, beginning with panatipata veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami.

o: a fine that monks pay for breaking a rule
a training step you take up yourself
a commandment that comes down from above

games.q: the first precept, word by word — tap the pairs.
p: I undertake, I take it up

s: the first precept is phrased as a command
it's phrased as a training the speaker takes up: sikkhapadam samadiyami, I undertake the training step.
pana means living beings, not only people
living, breathing beings: the snake counts.
in the story, the boys beat the snake for fun
they said they were afraid it would bite them.

games.q: you're walking past a ring of kids beating a snake with sticks. they say they're scared of it. what does the story have the Buddha do?
o: ask why, then point out the snake wants happiness just as they do.
warn them they'll be punished for it in their next life.
keep walking; it isn't his business what village kids do.
games.why: in the Dhammapada commentary he asks why, then teaches that whoever seeks happiness by harming beings who also want happiness won't find it. the reason is likeness, not threat.

practice: Stand and walk slowly for about a minute, a few steps at a time, watching where each foot lands, the way you would on a path where small things live.
Then sit for the rest of the bell, and if you'd like, say the line once: panatipata veramani sikkhapadam samadiyami.

wordCard.voice: Sikkhapada. A training step: a rule you take up yourself, not one handed down. Word ten of a little Pali.

orig.note: sikkhapadam in Devanagari letters: a training step, from sikkha, training, and pada, step.

carryVoice: Hold this one close: I undertake the training, a step I can take again tomorrow. Ten words in.

sources.q: All men tremble at punishment, all men fear death; remember that you are like unto them, and do not kill, nor cause slaughter.

sources.ref: Dhammapada 131–132 and the commentary's story (boys beating a snake with sticks in Savatthi)
sikkhā (training), pada (step, foothold), sikkhāpada (rule of training)
